key_claims: Neurodegenerative disorders involve interconnected cellular disturbances in redox regulation, mitochondrial function, neuroinflammation, and proteostasis rather than a single isolated lesion.

Plant-derived phytochemicals such as berberine, curcumin, ginsenosides, quercetin, and resveratrol influence multiple regulatory networks, including Nrf2 antioxidant responses and NF-κB inflammatory signalling.
Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation and histone modifications, help shape cellular responses and synaptic function under sustained stress.

Clinical translation of plant-derived neuroprotective compounds is currently hindered by low bioavailability, variable pharmacokinetics, limited blood-brain barrier penetration, and inconsistent botanical formulations.
limitations: Evidence from immortalised cell lines fails to replicate the full complexity of human neurodegenerative pathology, and in vitro findings frequently do not translate to in vivo outcomes.
Studies on complex botanical preparations often suffer from inconsistent phytochemical characterisation, missing voucher specimens, and variable cultivation or extraction methods.
The review notes that surrogate biological markers, such as blood DNA methylation clock scores, do not measure tissue-specific botanical, anti-inflammatory, joint, enzymatic, or mucosal benefits.
what_not_to_say: Do not claim that any specific botanical extract or phytochemical cures, prevents, or reverses neurodegenerative diseases in humans.
Do not present blood-based DNA methylation or epigenetic clock scores as direct measurements of tissue-specific anti-inflammatory, joint, enzymatic, or mucosal improvements.
Do not imply that single molecular targets are sufficient to treat neurodegenerative conditions, as the source emphasizes a multi-target network approach is required.
